prize_parts.citation: For incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, showing how exporting, foreign investment and reallocation across firms shape the gains from trade.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged in substance: one part, B038, with Melitz and Helpman. I reworded the citation after the exchange so that it names the mechanism (selection, exporting versus foreign investment, and reallocation) and makes no claim about the size of the welfare gains. Melitz (2003) and the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple work moved the unit of analysis in trade from countries and industries to firms. They gave a general-equilibrium account of why only some firms export, why trade liberalisation reallocates activity toward more productive firms, and why that is a distinct source of gains. The framework has had more than twenty years of testing on customs and production microdata. It has spread into macro, industrial organisation and development, which is why I see it as a mature discovery and not a recent one. On the chair's question about evidence, I would say that exporter premia and the size-productivity facts at the firm level were documented before the model, in the empirical work of Bernard, Jensen and others. The model's contribution is a unified explanation with new, testable implications for selection, reallocation and the choice between exporting and local production. That is what the citation claims. The credit set is also short. Melitz is the core model, and Helpman is central to the wider heterogeneous-firm agenda. I apply the same standard to every candidate: a distinct, mature discovery whose mechanism has been tested, and credit that can be assigned without implying others are lesser. I do not count support totals as merit, and the chair's tally of four explicit supporters for B038 does not enter my reasoning.
statement.case_against: The attribution risk remains real. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum have serious claims on closely related firm-level trade work and are outside the credited names. A Melitz-Helpman prize can be read as under-crediting the empirical and quantitative strands, and Redding's quantitative extensions are real even though I treat them as a later stage. The welfare magnitudes depend on elasticity and functional-form assumptions, so the citation cannot rest on any number. The 2008 prize on new trade theory also means the committee must state explicitly that firm selection is a separate step, not assume it. I think the argument for that is strong, but it is a judgement and the evidence does not settle it. Last, Helpman's credit on another candidate outside the shortlist has to be accounted for once if he is ever recognised.

responses.point: Friberg moved to B038 as his first choice and agrees on a Helpman-Melitz pairing without Redding. He qualifies the empirical case: exporter-premia facts were documented before the model, so the strongest confirmation is the selection and reallocation mechanism, not the size of the welfare gains, and the citation should not rest on a gains-from-trade number.
responses.response: I accept this qualification and have built it into the revised citation. It also gives a direct answer to the chair's question about what separates the founding contribution from the empirical exporter facts. The facts came first. The model supplied a single explanation with a productivity cutoff, reallocation and a welfare channel, plus testable implications on selection and on exporting versus foreign investment. The mechanism is much better supported than any magnitude. I would also tell colleagues that the elasticity sensitivity limits what the welfare numbers can bear, but it leaves the qualitative selection result largely intact. Friberg's reservation about Calvo pricing as a tractable device and not an empirical finding is a separate point about B015. I take it seriously there, and it does not change my view of B038.

responses.point: Hassler, who chairs and ranks B015 first with Woodford, Taylor and Calvo, treats the post-2021 inflation and the heterogeneous-agent critique as extensions and partial challenges and not refutations. He also says he would not oppose a Galí-Gertler pairing if the committee found it more defensible, and he lists B038 as an alternative.
responses.response: I agree B015 is fully mature and very influential, and that its attribution is a judgement call and not a settled fact. I move on the chair's symmetry question. I do apply one standard to both: the incremental discovery has to be distinct from what earlier prizes recognised. For B038 I think firm selection is distinct from the scale-economies and location results recognised in 2008. For B015 the corresponding question is how much is incremental to the earlier recognition of expectations and time consistency in macroeconomics, and I cannot answer that cleanly from the exchange. I also distinguish merit from prize design. I do not rank B015 below B038 on scientific weight. I rank it lower because the three names are contestable and the citation has to choose between origins and the canonical estimated model. If the committee settled on origin plus synthesis, I would see your trio as defensible. What would keep me with B038 is that its credit set needs no such choice. What would move me toward B015 is a clearly agreed citation, and evidence that the post-2021 inflation tested Calvo pricing and Taylor contracts specifically, not only the Phillips-curve specification.

responses.point: Strömberg prefers a two-name Kiyotaki-Moore prize, B050. He rejects adding Gertler because the accelerator line has a different lineage and Bernanke is already a laureate. He concedes that direct identification of the original amplification channel is mixed and that the 2022 prize may overlap.
responses.response: I already moved to the two-name version in round 1 and your argument still holds. Adding Gertler would blur both B050 and B015. I keep B050 as my first alternative because the attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist and the mechanism is foundational for macro-finance. In reply to the chair's question about direct evidence, I do not think the post-2008 record isolates the collateral-constraint channel from financial frictions in general. That is the main reason B050 sits second for me. I would not hold it to a stricter standard than B038. The two cases differ in kind: B038's mechanism has been tested directly on firm-level microdata, whereas B050's influence is mostly conceptual. If the committee judges clean attribution and conceptual foundation to outweigh that difference, I would regard a Kiyotaki-Moore outcome as defensible.

responses.point: Enflo prefers B038 with Melitz and Helpman, leaves Redding out to keep the citation focused, reads the 2008 prize as covering a different discovery, and accepts that the qualitative selection result is better supported than any welfare magnitude.
responses.response: I agree with this reading and with the framing that the committee should make the 2008 judgement explicitly. I would add one point on where we differ slightly. You locate Helpman's claim in the founding firm-heterogeneity contribution, which I accept. I would also tie it to the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple analysis of exporting versus foreign investment, because that is where his credit is least shared with the other candidates. On Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, I still do not resolve the concern. The three-name cap and the credited list restrict who can be named. I think the least bad response is a citation specific to the model of selection and its welfare implications, so that it does not appear to claim the whole firm-level trade literature.

responses.point: Krusell, who prefers B015 with Woodford, Taylor and Calvo, argues that dispersed credit complicates prize design without reducing scientific importance, and accepts that a committee valuing clean attribution above breadth could reasonably reverse his ordering. He lists B038 as his main alternative.
responses.response: I agree that dispersed credit does not make B015 scientifically weaker, and I try not to let attribution stand in for merit. My ranking reflects two separate judgements: both cases are mature and important, and B038 additionally has a credit set that needs no contestable choice. If the committee weights breadth of policy impact above attribution, we would rank them differently, and I do not think the evidence forces either weighting. I note that your co-authorship with me, and that of the chair, is disclosed and that I treat your arguments as evidence, not as independent confirmation of my own.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum have claims strong enough that a two-name Melitz-Helpman prize would be seen as incomplete, given that the three-name cap and credited list limit the options.
Whether the 2008 prize on new trade theory reduces the case for a second trade award, and whether the committee applies the same standard to B015's overlap with earlier macroeconomics prizes.
How much of the gains-from-trade result survives alternative elasticity and model assumptions, even if the qualitative selection and reallocation result is well supported.

Whether a Kiyotaki-Moore award (B050) or a B015 award with a settled citation is the stronger second candidate, which depends on how the committee weights clean attribution against breadth of influence and direct empirical identification.
I rely on general knowledge of the literature and the supplied round-1 files, and I have not independently verified any credit or citation record.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to the preferred part is apparent from the supplied profile: Melitz, Helpman and Redding are not listed among my co-authors or institutional contacts. I disclose a long-running collaboration with Peter Klenow (B016, not in my preferred configuration) and with Philippe Aghion, Antonin Bergeaud and Huiyu Li. I am a frequent co-author of Per Krusell (secretary) and a co-author of John Hassler (chair), and an IIES colleague of both. Both rank B015 first, and I treat their arguments as evidence only. My field of macroeconomics, growth and firm dynamics is adjacent to B038, which I disclose as a possible bias in how I weigh it. I have not adjudicated any of these ties.
